channel.title: FT – Fiction
channel.description: Fiction reviews and articles from the Financial Times.

item.title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman — the monsters in the garden
item.description: The award-winning novelist of ‘The Power’ returns with a curious mix of memoir, supernatural meditation and ecological conspiracy

item.title: The best books of the week
item.description: From Trump’s enablers to AI’s impact on kids and the last emperor of China. Plus inside the Venice Biennale, new novels by Sebastian Faulks and Rebecca F Kuang, Adam LeBor’s pick of thrillers — and our interview with Hernan Diaz

item.title: Interview.Hernan Diaz on his novel Ply — ‘The gesture of the book is very punkish’
item.description: The Pulitzer winner’s third novel continues his exploration of the character of America, from geographical space to capital and now technology and human connection

item.title: Farewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks — a plea for peace
item.description: Tracing a life of trauma and war, this involving novel is a characteristic hybrid, mixing moral questions and a murder mystery

item.title: Taipei Story — Rebecca F Kuang’s search for authenticity
item.description: The novelist’s exploration of Chinese-American identity sadly lacks the dynamism of her smash-hit ‘Yellowface’

item.title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère — the remarkable life of a literary grande dame
item.description: The French author draws a fascinating portrait of his mother, from the Russian Revolution to the heart of the Paris establishment

item.title: Battlefield realism and cosy espionage — our pick of the latest thrillers
item.description: Simon Conway, Alan Parks and Alex Gerlis draw on war zone heft while Mark Ezra and MJ Robotham have a welcome softer take on spy fiction

item.title: Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel — parallel visions of dystopia
item.description: This beautifully written novel portrays two equally terrifying views of the world in 2031 — total anarchy or safety under a repressive state

item.title: Denmark’s women on the edge: new fiction from Dorthe Nors and Helle Helle
item.description: Two newly translated novels exploring solitude, regret and lives not led are part of a compelling current wave of work from Danish female writers

item.title: Keeping it in the family — five books by debut authors
item.description: New novels about families warped by grief, history, violence and silence

item.title: Interview.Emma Cline on Switzy — ‘How would you survive those days, knowing what’s coming?’
item.description: The American novelist’s Booker-longlisted new novel follows a man with Alzheimer’s on his final journey to an assisted-dying clinic in Zurich

item.title: Making mischief with du Maurier: Rose Tremain reimagines the roots of Rebecca
item.description: ‘The Housekeeper’ fictionalises the story behind Daphne du Maurier’s gothic masterpiece — while a memoir by her grandson tells the unique family history that shaped her work

item.title: The Newer World — Sebastian Barry’s novel of the Black American slave experience
item.description: Set in the mid-1800s, the Irish author’s narrative blazes with an authenticity and poignancy that mitigates any risk of ‘cultural appropriation’

item.title: Obituary.Wendell Berry, writer and farmer, 1934-2026
item.description: The poet and essayist emerged from the 1960s counterculture movement to become a prominent voice in environmental activism and an outspoken critic of intensive agriculture

item.title: The Disappearers — Marlon James’s novel of righteous anger
item.description: The Booker Prize-winning author turns a planned theatre production in Jamaica into a compelling examination of homophobia, erasure and survival

item.title: Primeval and Other Times — Olga Tokarczuk’s exhilarating, genre-defying fairy tale
item.description: The Nobel Prize-winner’s kaleidoscopic novel, newly reissued, charts the stories of a Polish village — its people, plants, animals and angels — through the upheavals of the 20th century

item.title: Cold Sunset — the entertaining return of William Boyd’s reluctant spy
item.description: The third instalment in the Gabriel Dax series combines psychological tension and paranoia with irony and humour

item.title: Black September by Sandro Veronesi — a boy’s own story
item.description: The multi-award-winning Italian writer turns memory into drama in this warm, teasing account of an early-1970s adolescence

item.title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat — a family under fire
item.description: After witnessing a mall shooting, a Haitian-American mother questions her past, her relationships and the fragile safety she has built for her daughter

item.title: Agrippa by Robert Harris — a triumphant return to Rome?
item.description: Harris’s follow-up to the Cicero trilogy charts the fractious aftermath of Caesar’s death — and could have done with three volumes too

item.title: Life of M by Rachel Cusk — ‘no cruelty, no book’
item.description: The novelist turns the ethics of literary appropriation into her subject, asking what happens when an author makes art from other people’s lives — and pain

item.title: Élisabeth by Éric Rohmer — the novel that foretold the films
item.description: Newly translated, the director’s 1946 story of flirting, swimming and bickering in the French countryside heralds the screen classics to come

item.title: Irvine Welsh’s Can Nothing Save Us? — a family at war in Maga America
item.description: The ‘Trainspotting’ author’s well-rounded cast tell a story of envy, violence and generational conflict against the backdrop of Trump’s presidency

item.title: Etna by Paul Yoon — the horrors of war through a dog’s eyes
item.description: The brutal world of a battle-weary canine narrator is a piercing classic of survival with the feel of a modern parable

item.title: Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks — tuning into trauma
item.description: Pirate radio offers solace for a troubled young north London woman in the follow-up to Crooks’s acclaimed debut, ‘Fire Rush’
